title: The American Sign Museum is an illuminating trip through time
text:
The American Sign Museum is an illuminating trip through time
Founded in 1999, the American Sign Museum in Cincinnati pays homage to the artistry of the signs that have long attracted customers to businesses.
Kathy Greene and her husband, Tom, walked into a museum recently and found themselves transported to a small-town Main Street from their childhoods.
Museums are funny like that – time machines with rare powers of preservation, education, and nostalgia. The American Sign Museum in Cincinnati does this and more. Its collections hack your brain, tapping into memories of childhood road trips and family vacations gone by.
Walking through the museum’s life-size “Main Street USA” – with old-fashioned storefronts, a cinema hall marquee, and a McDonald’s sign from the 1960s – the couple and their guest, Ms. Greene’s brother, Gary Reedy, were spellbound.
The American Sign Museum’s collections hack your brain, tapping into memories of childhood road trips and family vacations gone by.
“We are old enough to remember these places,” says Mr. Greene, a retiree from Lebanon, Ohio, his face aglow from the neon light of a giant Howard Johnson’s restaurant sign from the 1960s.
Ms. Greene smiles. “I feel like I’m viewing this as a little child. It brings back good memories.”
Founded in 1999, the American Sign Museum pays homage to the artistry and craftsmanship of the signs that have long attracted customers to businesses, and that continue to connect many Americans with the bright lights, places, and memories of times past. Founder Tod Swormstedt, past publisher of Signs of the Times magazine, says he founded the museum as both a place to share his own personal collection of iconic signage and as a way to educate visitors about the role that signs play in our lives.
Erin Holland, director of education and engagement for the museum, says that because signs are such everyday objects, they are often overlooked. “These are artifacts,” she says. “There is a lot of history behind these signs, and they are worth saving.”
With 800 signs, 1,500 photographs, 175 pieces of artwork, and 300 tools of the sign-making trade, the museum’s collection reaches different audiences in different ways, Ms. Holland says. “Our older folks can share stories of what these signs meant to them, and young people can get an appreciation for the way things were, the beauty of the past.”
Mr. Swormstedt wanted visitors to see how the American sign-making industry changed as American society changed. Hand-painted wooden signs and porcelain yielded to neon during the Great Depression, when Americans were craving a bit of light in their lives. After World War II, burger joints and motels competed to attract families exploring America along the new interstate highway system.
Signs speak volumes about America’s changing dream: well-fed boys serving burgers after years of depression and war, or mechanical satellites twirling above shopping malls in the midst of America’s space race with the Soviet Union.
The museum has restored many signs to make them functional again. A spinning globe from the Earl Scheib auto painting company in Compton, California, for instance, was repainted, and its car-shaped neon lights were reworked at the museum’s neon shop. But the restoration team left the entry and exit holes for a bullet that was shot through the globe.
